gold_trajectory:
# Detailed Simulated Retrieval Trajectory · 2-2-B01

## Step 01 · Formulate instrument hypothesis from the three-piece hinged structure

**Action:** First observe the overall construction of the current input, then combine confirmed components into search terms. You can try `antique hinged writing slate grooved metal blind` or `braille slate two different grids`; these are retrieval examples.

**Evidence Observation:** The image does not show a single ruler: three slender metal plates are hinged at the ends; the middle, brighter plate surface has continuous parallel horizontal grooves; the near-side perforated plate has two rows of wider rectangular holes (top and bottom), while the far-side plate has a denser array of tall holes. Protruding positioning components are also visible on the plate surfaces. These structures support the hypothesis of a "writing slate for clamping paper and guiding a stylus." The photo's oblique angle and occlusions do not allow reliably counting all hole rows on the far side, nor can all materials be determined directly from color.

**Result of this step:** Focus the search on tactile writing tools for the blind, especially combination slates with different guide holes; the specific name still awaits confirmation from museum text and the original photo.

## Step 02 · Distinguish the combination slate from standard Ballu slates in specialized collections

**Action:** Enter Ballu-related records from the APH Writing collection catalog, while checking single-purpose pocket slates and desk slates, comparing actual construction rather than just titles.

https://sites.aph.org/museum-virtual-exhibit/vex2/toc.htm

https://sites.aph.org/museum-virtual-exhibit/vex2/2E7A5222-77D8-469A-92F2-351016232620.htm

https://sites.aph.org/museum-virtual-exhibit/vex2/89EF692A-D359-45F3-B2D2-572291221460.htm

https://sites.aph.org/museum-virtual-exhibit/vex2/C7697C3A-3E34-4358-A263-369139754553.htm

**Evidence Observation:** The preserved APH pages describe the first two items as 9-dot and 10-dot Ballu pocket slates respectively; both have slender hole plates and grooved base plates, which can explain part of the subject image. The unfolded photo of the 10-dot pocket slate is particularly similar, but it has only two pieces (hole plate and grooved base plate) and cannot explain the extra two rows of wide-hole guide plates in the subject image. The desk model has a large-area grooved plate, outer frames with positioning holes on both sides, and a horizontal guide ruler, which differs from the three-piece narrow-long-plate structure in the subject image. There is no need here to treat 9-dot and 10-dot as features that must be identified dot-by-dot from the subject image.

https://sites.aph.org/museum-virtual-exhibit/vex2/images/122ff401-452a-4226-b8b7-613568293170.jpg

https://sites.aph.org/museum-virtual-exhibit/vex2/images/87e08977-0100-41f5-b656-599606957370.jpg

**Result of this step:** Standard Ballu pocket slates are reasonable neighbors but cannot cover all visible structures; continue checking combination models in the same catalog without expanding to an exhaustive list of all historical writing slates.

## Step 03 · Close identification using original photos and explicit names from the target collection

**Action:** Check the APH entry for `Ballu and braille slate` and compare its unfolded original photo item-by-item with the input.

https://sites.aph.org/museum-virtual-exhibit/vex2/F0E4F497-334C-418C-9562-325254743864.htm

https://sites.aph.org/museum-virtual-exhibit/vex2/images/4f311aca-856a-4a66-8bd7-099741390400.jpg

**Evidence Observation:** The museum's original photo and the subject image share the same unfolding angle, front and rear sets of guide holes, the silver-bright horizontal-grooved middle plate, and the location of end wear, indicating a correspondence to the same photo. The page explicitly writes it as a hinged Ballu and braille dual-purpose pocket slate: one piece for two rows of Braille, one piece for high-position Ballu guide dots, with a shared middle plate featuring horizontal grooves and positioning pins. The three-piece structure described in the literature matches the visible layout in the input. The precise hole counts given by the museum belong to catalog specifications; there is no need to pretend they were counted from the oblique photo.

**Result of this step:** The target name and specific combination structure have both been supported by direct evidence. Other photos from APH belong to the same collection evidence chain and do not serve as independent verification from multiple institutions; historical plates and Ballu tools from other collections also need not be treated as mandatory steps.

## Step 04 · Answer according to the granularity of the question and stop retrieval

**Action:** Convert the museum's English name into the specific instrument name required by the current question, retaining both Ballu and Braille uses and the pocket-style construction.

**Evidence Observation:** "Braille slate" is too broad, while "Ballu pocket slate" omits the visible second Braille guide plate; the name of the target entry and the three-piece construction are sufficient to support the combination model. There is no need to add manufacturing year, collection number, or dot-by-dot counting conclusions.

**Result of this step:** The evidence is sufficient; stop retrieval.

**Formal Answer:**

Ballu–Braille dual-purpose pocket slate
